```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
strava_runs <- read_csv("data/strava_runs.csv")
```

```{r}
data_5k_10k <- strava_runs %>%
  mutate(
    event = case_when(
      distance..m. > 4998 & distance..m. < 5015  ~ "5k",
      distance..m. > 9998 & distance..m. < 10015 ~ "10k",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(event))
```


## Exercise 1

When you fill the missing part, remove the # symbol before running the code chunk and eval=FALSE

```{r ex1a, out.width="80%", eval=FALSE}
data_5k_10k %>% 
  filter(gender=="M") %>%
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = average.heart.rate..bpm.)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 20)
```


```{r ex1a(2), out.width="80%"}
male_bc <- data_5k_10k |>
  filter(gender == "M") |>
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.))
male_bc |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(average.heart.rate..bpm.),
    median = median(average.heart.rate..bpm.),
    sd = sd(average.heart.rate..bpm.)
  )
# 1(a) This bar chart shows that distribution of average heart rates among male runners is approximately normal. Most runners have average heart rates between 140 and 165 bpm, with the highest frequency occurring around 145–150 bpm. The mean and median are both 148 bpm, indicating that the centre of the distribution is around this value.The standard deviation is 17.2 bpm, suggesting some variation in average heart rates among runners.


```


```{r ex1b, out.width="80%"}
Female_bc <- data_5k_10k |>
  filter(gender == "F") |>
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.))
Female_bc |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(average.heart.rate..bpm.),
    median = median(average.heart.rate..bpm.),
    sd = sd(average.heart.rate..bpm.)
  )
# 1(b) The histogram for female runners appears to be possibly bimodal, with two local peaks around 145–150 bpm and 165–170 bpm. Compared with male runners, female runners have a higher average heart rate, with a mean of 156 bpm compared with 148 bpm for males. The standard deviation is lower for females (13.2 bpm) than for males (17.2 bpm), suggesting that heart rates are less dispersed in the female sample. However, since the female sample is smaller, further analysis would be needed to determine whether the distribution is genuinely bimodal.


```

## Exercise 2

```{r ex2a, out.width = "80%"}
data_5k_10k <- strava_runs |>
     mutate(
         distance_km = distance..m. / 1000,
         pace = (elapsed.time..s. / 60) / distance_km,
         race_distance = case_when(
             abs(distance_km - 5) <= 0.2 ~ "5K",
             abs(distance_km - 10) <= 0.2 ~ "10K",
             TRUE ~ NA_character_
         )
     ) %>%
     filter(!is.na(race_distance), !is.na(gender), !is.na(pace))
ggplot(data_5k_10k, aes(x = race_distance, y = pace)) +
     geom_boxplot() +
     facet_wrap(~ gender) +
     labs(
         title = "Running Pace by Distance and Gender",
         x = "Race Distance",
         y = "Pace (minutes per km)"
     )
```

```{r ex2b, out.width = "80%"}
# The mean pace is lower for male runners than for female runners at both distances, showing that male runners generally run faster. For both genders, the pace is slightly higher for 5K runs than for 10K runs, indicating that the runners in this dataset tend to have a faster pace over 10K. Both genders also show several high-pace outliers, means that considerable variation in running performance.


```


## Exercise 3

```{r ex3a, out.width = "80%"}
athlete_avg <- strava_runs |>
     group_by(athlete) |>
     summarise(
         avg_distance = mean(distance..m., na.rm = TRUE) / 1000,
     )
long_dis_runner <- athlete_avg |>
  filter(avg_distance > 13) |>
  mutate(runner_type = "Long-distance runner")
short_dis_runner <- athlete_avg |>
  filter(avg_distance < 7) |>
  mutate(runner_type = "Short-distance runner")
runner_groups <- full_join(
  long_dis_runner |> select(athlete, runner_type),
  short_dis_runner |> select(athlete, runner_type),
  by = "athlete"
)
runner_groups <- runner_groups |>
  mutate(
    runner_type = coalesce(runner_type.x, runner_type.y)
  ) |>
  select(athlete, runner_type)
data_7k_13k <- strava_runs |>
  left_join(
    runner_groups,
    by = "athlete"
  )
data_7k_13k <- data_7k_13k |>
  filter(
    !is.na(runner_type),
    !is.na(distance..m.),
    !is.na(elapsed.time..s.),
    elapsed.time..s. > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    distance_km = distance..m. / 1000,
    Run_average_speed = distance..m. / elapsed.time..s.
  )
ggplot(
  data_7k_13k,
  aes(
    x = distance_km,
    y = Run_average_speed,
    colour = runner_type
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2)+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Long-distance runner" = "orange",
      "Short-distance runner" = "forestgreen"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Speed vs Distance for Long- and Short-Distance Runners",
    subtitle = "Groups based on average running distance: >13 km vs <7 km",
    x = "Run distance (km)",
    y = "Run average speed (m/s)",
  )



```
```{r ex3b, out.width = "80%"}
# This graph suggests that long-distance runners generally maintain a relatively stable average speed as running distance increases, whereas short-distance runners show a more decrease in average speed. This shows that long-distance runners may be better able to maintain their pace over longer distances.
```
